item.title: Wisconsin court rejects prenup after husband's monthly income surpasses $81,000
item.description: In Wisconsin, a marriage contract ignited a lengthy divorce dispute marked by staggering wealth disparities. After almost two decades, Tracy Marie Chernick managed to contest the fairness of their initial agreement. The Wisconsin Court of Appeals determined that Ryan David Chernick had withheld crucial financial details prior to their wedding.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Archaeologists in a West Texas rock shelter found a hunting kit left untouched for about 6,500 years
item.description: In a remarkable archaeological find in West Texas, researchers uncovered a hunting kit that dates back approximately 6,000 years. The collection features various stone and wooden foreshafts, along with essential hunting tools, including a partial atlatl, which is an ancient spear-throwing apparatus. The diversity of materials suggests varying time periods, unlocking valuable insights into the lifestyles and surroundings of these ancient communities.
item.dc:creator: World Desk

item.title: Virginia worker wins disability benefits seven years after 20-foot construction fall
item.description: A Virginia appeals court upheld the temporary total disability benefits for construction worker Olegario Felipe Valles. Valles had suffered serious injuries from a 20-foot fall while working in 2019 and underwent spinal fusion surgery. The court supported the Virginia Workers' Compensation Commission's decision that he was unable to return to work. The employer's appeal to terminate his benefits was rejected due to insufficient evidence.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Mayo Clinic to pay $906K in back wages over unpaid pre-shift work
item.description: Mayo Clinic has committed to paying over $906,000 in back wages to employees after an investigation uncovered they were required to perform preparatory tasks without compensation prior to their shifts. To rectify this, the clinic has revamped its timekeeping practices to guarantee that all work is accurately compensated, particularly addressing the daily initiation of computer tasks.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Three of five adult baboon skulls found in Chad bear puncture marks from eagle talons
item.description: In a groundbreaking study, researchers in Chad have uncovered puncture marks on baboon skulls, suggesting that eagles may prey on these large primates. Out of five examined skulls, three displayed signs typical of eagle talon strikes. This startling discovery raises questions about baboons' vulnerability to aerial predators and encourages a reassessment of early hominin interactions with such threats, potentially reshaping our understanding of primate evolution.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: North Dakota man claimed 1993 map gave access over neighbours' land; court rejected easement claim
item.description: In a recent legal clash in North Dakota, landowner Rudra Tamm faced a setback as the North Dakota Supreme Court dismissed his case concerning access roads through adjacent properties. The court determined Tamm did not adequately demonstrate an easement and failed to provide sufficient evidence of the required deed. His appeal based on historical usage was also declined, ultimately reaffirming his neighbors' rights over the contested access paths.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: A Virginia farm that has been cultivated for more than 375 years is now permanently protecting 1,145 acres from development, including 452 acres of active farmland and 4.5 miles of river shoreline
item.description: Conservation efforts have been successful in protecting 1,145 acres of Retreat Farm in Hanover County, Virginia. This area includes prime farmland, wetlands, and river shoreline along the Pamunkey River. The Capital Region Land Conservancy collaborated with the USDA's NRCS to secure a permanent conservation easement. The agreement ensures the land remains agricultural, preventing future disruptive development. This initiative highlights the importance of preserving historical and ecological landscapes for future generations.
item.dc:creator: World Desk

item.title: Canada's top court upholds Quebec's religious symbols ban for public sector workers
item.description: In a significant ruling, Canada's Supreme Court has upheld most aspects of Quebec's Bill 21, enforcing a ban on public employees wearing religious symbols. This decision reaffirms the provincial government's stance on secularism despite ongoing lawsuits. However, the court identified certain provisions on face coverings for elected officials as unconstitutional.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Louisiana court awards 3 children $301,000 after father takes late wife's $623,274 settlement
item.description: Lionel Adams Sr. from Louisiana faced a setback as the court denied his appeal concerning his late wife Ora Jean Adams' asbestos settlement funds. The verdict revealed that the funds, which were not legally gifted to him prior to her passing, remained with their three children. The court ruled that he must pay them over $301,000, honoring their mother's intent to distribute the money equally.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Pennsylvania widow keeps $6,000 home after court rejects stepchildren's inheritance claim
item.description: Jane L. Shellhammer, a widow from Pennsylvania, has successfully defended her right to remain in her family home following her husband's passing. Although his children attempted to lay claim to the property, the Pennsylvania Superior Court determined that the couple owned the house as tenants by the entirety. Consequently, Jane retains sole ownership of the Palmerton residence, a place she has cherished for over 45 years.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Australian worker wins A$17,861 after employer fails to consider vacant role before AI-linked redundancy
item.description: An Australian contracts administrator faced dismissal as the employer attributed this to the reduced necessity for his role due to AI tools. However, after the employee filed an unfair dismissal claim, the Fair Work Commission awarded compensation, highlighting the employer's neglect in exploring redeployment options. While the redundancy was justified, the company failed to conduct a fair process, particularly as the employee had expressed interest in other roles.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: From $24.6 billion to $1.7 billion: Billionaire Carl Icahn loses 93% of his fortune in five years
item.description: Billionaire Carl Icahn's fortune has fallen from $24.6 billion to about $1.7 billion in five years, even as major US stock indexes surged. Mounting debt, losses on market bets and a looming $1.4 billion bond repayment have put fresh pressure on the veteran investor's business empire, marking a dramatic reversal for one of Wall Street's most feared dealmakers.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: In 1947, architect John Lautner designed a Hollywood Hills home with a roof supported by a three-point steel structure; the preserved two-bedroom Polin House is now listed for $2.85 million
item.description: Renowned architect John Lautner's striking house from 1947 has hit the market, offering a distinctive two-bedroom, two-bathroom experience in the vibrant Hollywood Hills. Spanning 1,342 square feet and priced at $2,850,000, this home features a groundbreaking steel roof truss design that provides an uninterrupted interior space. With outdoor terraces enhancing the living area, this listing is a rare chance to own a piece of architectural history.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: New Zealand Earthship built from 1,300 tyres and 7,000 bottles goes on sale after TV fame
item.description: For sale in New Zealand's scenic Coromandel region, a distinct four-bedroom Earthship home composed of recycled tyres and glass bottles awaits new owners. This eco-conscious abode, featuring solar power and passive heating, was constructed in 2015 and has gained popularity following its showcase on Grand Designs New Zealand. Owners Gus Anning and Sarah Rowe are transitioning to the Bay of Islands, seeking individuals who will honor their sustainable dream.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: UK DWP takes online services offline after cyber incident, but benefit payments continue
item.description: On November 27, 2026, a significant cyber incident struck the UK's Department for Work and Pensions, leading to the suspension of online services for Universal Credit and other benefits as a precautionary measure. Although regular payments remained unaffected, users faced difficulties accessing their accounts and processing applications. Cybersecurity professionals cautioned about potential scams aimed at those caught up in this disruption.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: London's 1814 Beer Flood: Brewery disaster killed eight in bizarre tragedy
item.description: On October 17, 1814, a catastrophic explosion at the Horse Shoe Brewery in London unleashed tons of beer onto the streets, tragically claiming the lives of eight individuals, including many women and children. Rescuers faced an arduous task as they navigated the wreckage to reach survivors trapped amid the ruins.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Norse Atlantic risks losing all 12 Dreamliners as funding crisis threatens bankruptcy
item.description: Norse Atlantic Airways finds itself in dire straits, grappling with severe financial challenges stemming from lease terminations for its Boeing 787 fleet. After halting all operations on November 26 due to a precarious cash position, the airline is now on the brink of bankruptcy. Amidst disputes over lease validity and the pursuit of emergency funding, its stock has plummeted, leaving its future operations hanging in the balance.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: BC court rejects couple's claim to a lakeside access road under a 1997 agreement
item.description: Jeno and Luminita Fabian attempted to assert access rights to their property by using a road on a developer's land. However, the Supreme Court of British Columbia ruled against them regarding the easement agreement from 1997. The court determined that the disputed road section was not covered under that easement. Their alternative request for a statutory easement was also rejected under property law.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk
